Bunun haricinde hiçbir şekilde uyuşturucu madde kullanmadım. Uyuşturucu madde kullanmadım. Satan kimseyi de tanımam. Üzerime atılı suçlamaları kabul etmiyorum.” dedi.
Burcu Özberk ise ifadesinde aylık gelirinin 300 bin TL olduğunu söyledi. Telefon şifresini savcılığa veren Özberk ifadesinde, “Genelde yoğun olarak dizi çekimleri olur. Onun için işten eve evden işe olarak çalışırım. Bu nedenle geceleri genelde dışarı çıkmam. Dolayısıyla uyuşturucu içilen ortamlarda da bulunmadım, bulunmam da. Ben uyuşturucu madde veya yeşil reçeteli herhangi bir madde kullanmam. Üzerime atılı suçlamaları kabul etmiyorum. Derhal salıverilerek hakkında kovuşturmaya yer olmadığına dair karar verilmesini istiyorum. Ayrıca cep telefonumun şifresini verdiğim için bir an önce incelenerek tarafıma iade edilmesini istiyorum. Cep telefonumda işimle ilgili senaryolar mevcuttur. Bu nedenle mümkünse özel bilirkişiye incelemesi yapılarak tarafıma teslim edilmesini talep ediyorum.” dedi.

ABD Federal İletişim Komisyonu (FCC) uzay, havacılık ve yapay zeka şirketi SpaceX’in uzayda veri merkezleri oluşturmak amacıyla 1 milyon uydu fırlatma talebini onayladı.
FCC’nin açıklamasına göre ABD tarihinde ilk kez uzayda veri merkezi kümesi kurulması için yetki verildi.
Devasa miktarda veriyi işleyecek yörüngesel hesaplama modüllerini konuşlandırması için SpaceX’e izin verildi; sistemin FCC’nin ‘yörünge enkazı’ kurallarına uygun olarak çalışacağı öne sürüldü.
Şirket yapay zeka nedeniyle hızla artan talebi karşılamak için 1 milyona kadar uydudan oluşan ‘Starmind’ kümesi kuracakmış. Yedekleme ve acil durum telemetri, takip ve komuta işlemleri için de radyo frekansı bağlantıları kullanılacak, uydular arası optik bağlantılar da bu iletişimle desteklenecek.
FCC Başkanı Brendan Carr, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump’ın liderliğinde yapay zeka teknolojisinin getirdiği fırsat ve sağlayacağı faydaları güvenceye almak için çalıştığını vurguladı: “Bu hamle, Amerika’nın liderliğine ve büyümesine güç verecek bilgi işlem altyapısı için cesur ve yeni bir ufuk açıyor.”
Carr, veri merkezlerinin ABD’nin yapay zeka alanındaki liderliği için önem taşıdığını öne sürerek şöyle devam etti :
“SpaceX ve kendi yörüngesel veri merkezleri üzerinde çalışan pek çok rakibi, bilgi işlem kapasitesini Dünya’nın dışına taşıyarak çağın gereğini yerine getiriyor. Bu, uzay ve ileri teknolojideki gücümüzü birleştirebilecek, ekonomik liderliğimizi pekiştirecek ve ülkemizdeki refahı artıracak türden bir Amerikan marifetidir.”
1957’de Sputnik 1 uzaya fırlatılan ilk uydu olmuştu . Sky News’ün haberine göre uzaydaki uydu sayısı 17 bini buldu.
Uzayda en az 11 bin uydusu bulunan milyarder Elon Musk’ın SpaceX şirketinin 1 milyon uyduyu nasıl yerleştireceğiyse henüz belli değil.

The best meal delivery services and meal kits are the ones that make your home life easier—and maybe make dinner something to look forward to rather than to dread. I didn't actually expect to appreciate meal kits as much as I do, as someone who likes to cook and worked as a food critic on both coasts for more than a decade.
I've found that the best meal kits helped me climb out of a cooking rut of turning to the same dishes—and the same flavors—over and over. After testing every major meal delivery service over the past two years, I've narrowed the field to just a few of the best options for each family and diet. Quite simply, the best meals I've eaten from a meal kit have come from Marley Spoon , which offers a path to genuinely good home-cooked meals on nights when I might otherwise feel uninspired.
But depending on your priorities, other meal delivery services might be the best for you. I've found that Home Chef offers the greatest flexibility for busy families while keeping prices affordable. EveryPlate is the best meal kit for people on a tight budget. For a healthful, tailored diet (including an option on true gluten-free meals), I recommend Green Chef . If you'd rather not cook at all, CookUnity is the best prepared-meal delivery service I've ever had the pleasure to warm up.
I assessed each meal plan's recipes, breadth of selection, sourcing, ease of preparation, convenience, organization, packaging, high-quality ingredients, and suitability for different eating restrictions and needs. I also tested the best new and innovative meal kits for those looking for alternatives to Blue Apron or HelloFresh's long-standing meal delivery services. And not for nothing, I sorted out some often maddeningly nontransparent pricing. Here are the best delivery meal subscriptions I've tried.
Be sure to check out my investigation into whether sometimes Meal Kits Are Cheaper Than Groceries when trying out new recipes, and WIRED's related guides, including the Best Plant-Based Meal Kits , Best Food Gifts You Can Buy Online , Best Coffee Subscriptions , and Best Delivery Chocolate Boxes .
Updated September 2026: After a new round of testing, I've listed Green Chef as my favorite meal kit for clean ingredients and dietary restrictions. I also retested CookUnity and confirmed its place as the best prepared meal delivery service. I likewise retested and updated my descriptions of Factor prepared meals and GardenCup’s salad kit, and added information about HelloFresh’s new recipe app and Blue Apron’s new packaging and partnership with Misfits Market.
In the decade since it was introduced on American shores, the strength of the Martha Stewart–endorsed Marley Spoon meal delivery service has remained steadfast: It's the cooking.
The best individual meals I've cooked among the 20 or so kits I've tested in the past two years have come from Marley Spoon . A hearty Hungarian-influenced creamy mushroom chicken , a boldly Cajun-spiced whitefish, or a delicate eggplant parm. Those meals are still on the menu.
But Marley Spoon has also been evolving of late. Over the past year or two, the German-founded meal kit has added more menu items, more cosmopolitan meals with global flavors, and a greater variety of preparation times that now include a lot of 15-minute meals. It's done this without raising the price of the meal kit this year—no mean feat amid rising food and shipping costs.
The classic “Martha's Best” recipes are now augmented by meals that emphasize convenience and global flavors. A third of the menu is now prepared, ready-to-heat meals. I see more 15-minute dishes and tray oven bakes. Marley Spoon also seems to have broadened its international fare, with takes on a Moroccan-spiced apricot and beef tagine and Indian-influenced keema matar that's as easy to make as garam masala sloppy Joe.
Still, more than other meal kits, Marley remains devoted to classical cooking technique—the sort they teach in culinary school and on Martha Stewart's TV shows. This is no accident. When the German-founded meal kit arrived in the US, it did so with the cooking maven's endorsement and a lot of her recipes and techniques. Recipes often call for light seasoning throughout the process—not all at once. A kale and sausage soup, deeply savory, might be balanced with acid from a surprising splash of red wine vinegar.
Marley Spoon is more honest than most meal kits about the time it actually takes to cook a recipe. While your 15-minute meal might acccctually still require 20 minutes, it definitely won't take 30 or 40. There is one point of inconvenience with Marley, one that might help keep the company's prices from climbing: Unlike other top-line kits, Marley sends your ingredients jumbled in a box, which reduces packaging waste but also leaves you hunting for the right spice mix or dried ingredient. The meat sourcing also isn't as transparent as some kits.
Like Blue Apron and others, Marley Spoon has recently partnered with food delivery service Misfits Market after its previous US partner, FreshRealm, filed for Chapter 11 protection. I'll be testing and monitoring to make sure Marley keeps earning its spot at the top of this list. While maintaining value, Marley Spoon offers genuinely good cooking and acts as a little school in culinary techniques. Some other meal kits on this list might offer more flexibility. Marley offers a firm backbone.
Home Chef lets you do pretty much whatever you want. Do you want two servings of two recipes, but eight servings of a third? No problem. Did you want to add an oven-ready steak meal for six to this week's order, and only this week's order? Also not a problem. Have a large family? Home Chef offers a cheaper family plan for batched family meals. Want fewer meals this week than your typical order? Each meal will cost a little more, but you can still cut back your order on the fly without canceling.
More than any other meal kit I've tested, Home Chef is optimized for convenience, down to the transparent plastic bags that house each meal's ingredients. The recipes are finely detailed, with easy-to-follow instructions. Nutrition and allergens are listed in even finer detail online. Each recipe is classed according to difficulty, and even the theoretically highfalutin’ “culinary collection” meals aren't hard to make or dauntingly culinary—mayhaps a stuffed chicken breast, perhaps some gnocchi.
It's not for nothing that WIRED previously listed Home Chef as the best meal kit for beginner chefs: The recipe instructions are full of little hand-holds and added advice. That said, the meals I've tried weren't quite as sophisticated and tasty as those you'll get from my top pick, Marley Spoon, nor as varied and interesting as HelloFresh. One “culinary” meal was basically a stuffed burger with seasoned fries.
But convenience, flexibility, and good administration count for a lot in this world. So do relatively low prices, at $10 a meal on most standard plans and $8 a plate for the kid-friendly family plan. If you've got a family life with meal demands that change from week to week—which is a lot of the people looking to meal kits to solve problems—Home Chef may be precisely the meal kit you need.
I'll put it simply: CookUnity is the only prepared-meal delivery service I've tried that has ever delivered a meal better than local restaurant takeout. Specifically, from the Seattle kitchen run by chef Gaurav Raj, I've tried multiple Indian gravies from butter chicken to chicken lababdar that tasted better than I could get at the Punjabi restaurant down the street.
Prepared meal delivery services promise a hunger-squelching holy grail: fresh meals, delivered to your door in a box that's ready to heat and eat, minus all the effort of actually cooking it. But my results from many other prepared-meal delivery services have been mixed. Indeed, some struggle to better the TV dinners they resemble. The reason CookUnity has been a big standout is its unique business model.

İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığının ünlü isimlere yönelik yürüttüğü uyuşturucu ve fuhuş soruşturmasında, savcılık işlemleri tamamlanan şarkıcı Ceylan Kaya tutuklandı. Aralarında Burcu Özberk, Özcan Deniz ve Murat Ceylan'ın da bulunduğu 9 şüpheli ise yurt dışına çıkış yasağı şeklinde adli kontrol tedbiri uygulanarak serbest bırakıldı.
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı tarafından yürütülen uyuşturucu ve fuhuş soruşturması kapsamında gözaltına alınan şüphelilerin savcılık işlemleri tamamlandı. Şarkıcı Ceylan Kaya, tutuklama talebiyle; aralarında tanınmış isimlerin de bulunduğu 9 şüpheli ise adli kontrol talebiyle nöbetçi sulh ceza hakimliğine sevk edildi.
Hakimlikteki işlemlerinin ardından şarkıcı Ceylan Kaya, “suçtan kaynaklanan malvarlığı değerlerini aklama” suçundan tutuklanarak cezaevine gönderildi.
Soruşturma kapsamında adli kontrol talebiyle hakimliğe sevk edilen Burcu Özberk, Özcan Deniz, Murat Ceylan, Ufuk Gündoğdu, Deniz Sözen, Murat Başoğlu, Deniz Çakır Baykal, İbrahim Yılmaz ve Onur Yüksel hakkında karar verildi.
Hakimlik, 9 şüpheli hakkında yurt dışına çıkış yasağı şeklinde adli kontrol tedbiri uygulanmasına karar verdi. Şüpheliler, kararın ardından serbest bırakıldı.
İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığından yapılan açıklamada, soruşturmanın Kaçakçılık, Narkotik ve Ekonomik Suçlar Soruşturma Bürosu tarafından yürütüldüğü belirtildi. Soruşturmanın; “fuhuş”, “uyuşturucu veya uyarıcı madde ticareti”, “uyuşturucu veya uyarıcı madde temin etme” ile “uyuşturucu madde kullanma veya bulundurma” suçlarını kapsadığı bildirildi.
Açıklamada, şüphelilerin savunmaları, bilgi sahibi kişilerin tanık sıfatıyla alınan ifadeleri, ele geçirilen cep telefonları ve dijital materyaller üzerinde yapılan bilirkişi incelemeleri sonucunda hazırlanan raporlar ile gizli tanık anlatımlarının değerlendirildiği kaydedildi.
Başsavcılığın açıklamasında, uyuşturucu madde kullanıldığı veya bulundurulduğu yönünde edinilen şüphe üzerine başlatılan soruşturma kapsamında 35 şüpheli hakkında gözaltı kararı verildiği belirtilerek, soruşturmanın tüm yönleriyle sürdüğü ifade edildi.

WhatsApp , kullanıcıların mesajlarını ileri bir tarihte gönderilmek üzere ayarlamasını sağlayan mesaj zamanlama özelliğini herkese açtı. Şirketin resmi blogunda duyurduğu özellikle mesajlar, 10 dakika ile 14 gün sonrası arasında istenen bir tarih ve saatte otomatik olarak gönderilebilecek. WhatsApp, özelliği kullanıcıların en çok talep ettiği özelliklerden biri olarak tanımladı.
Mesaj zamanlama, önümüzdeki haftalarda Android ve iPhone kullanıcılarına dünya genelinde sunulacak. WhatsApp'ın deneme sürümlerini takip eden WABetaInfo'ya göre özellik aşamalı olarak açılacağı için herkes aynı anda göremeyebilir. Seçeneği henüz göremeyen kullanıcılara bir sonraki güncellemede gelmesi bekleniyor.
Mesaj zamanlamak için mesaj yazıldıktan ya da fotoğraf veya video seçildikten sonra gönder tuşuna basılı tutmak yeterli. Açılan ekrandan tarih ve saat seçilip onaylanınca mesaj sıraya alınıyor. Özellik metin mesajlarının yanı sıra fotoğraf, video ve bağlantılar için de kullanılabiliyor. Ancak fotoğraf ve videolar tek tek zamanlanabiliyor.
Zamanlanan mesaj WhatsApp'ın sunucusuna gönderiliyor ve seçilen saatte buradan karşı tarafa iletiliyor. Bu sayede gönderenin telefonu o sırada kapalı ya da internete bağlı olmasa bile mesaj zamanında gidiyor. Mesajlar, yalnızca gönderen ve alıcının görebildiği uçtan uca şifrelemeyle korunuyor. Alıcı, mesajın önceden zamanlandığını göremiyor.
Özellik birebir sohbetlerin yanı sıra grup sohbetlerinde de çalışıyor. Ancak gruba zamanlanan mesaj, yalnızca zamanlama yapıldığı sırada grupta bulunan üyelere ulaşıyor. Mesaj zamanlandıktan sonra gruba katılanlar bu mesajı almıyor.
Zamanlanan mesajlar, her sohbetin bilgi ekranında ayrı bir bölümde listeleniyor. Kullanıcılar mesajlarını gönderilmeden önce buradan görebiliyor ve silebiliyor. Zamanlanan bir mesaj silindiğinde alıcıya herhangi bir bildirim gitmiyor. Rakip uygulamalardan Telegram ve Apple'ın iMessage'ı bu özelliği uzun süredir sunuyordu.
WhatsApp ayrıca hareketli çıkartmalara ses ekleme özelliğini test etmeye başladı. WABetaInfo'ya göre "sesli çıkartma" adı verilen özellikte kullanıcılar galerilerindeki videoları hareketli çıkartmaya çevirip kendi seslerini, videonun orijinal sesini ya da kahkaha, kedi mırlaması gibi hazır ses efektlerini ekleyebiliyor. Ses kaydı en fazla 5 saniye sürebiliyor.
Alıcı çıkartmadaki ses simgesine dokunduğunda ses çalıyor ve üç kez tekrarlandıktan sonra duruyor. Sesli çıkartmalar şimdilik yalnızca bazı Android ve iPhone deneme kullanıcılarına açık. Özellik için WhatsApp'tan henüz resmi bir açıklama yapılmadı.

Ünlülere yönelik yürütülen soruşturma kapsamında şüpheliler arasında yer alan şarkıcı Ceylan Kaya, suçtan kaynaklanan mal varlığı değerlerini aklama suçlamasıyla tutuklandı. Soruşturma kapsamında gözaltına alınan Özcan Deniz, Deniz Çakır ve Burcu Özberk'in de aralarında bulunduğu 9 kişinin adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakılmasıyla birlikte Ceylan Kaya'nın hayatı ve kariyeri merak konusu oldu. Peki, Ceylan Kaya kimdir, kaç yaşında, nereli ve evli mi?
Ceylan Kaya, şarkıcılığın yanı sıra sunuculuk ve oyunculuk alanlarında da çalışmalar yapan bir sanatçıdır. Sahne performansları ve televizyon programlarıyla tanınan Kaya, müzik çalışmalarını dijital platformlar ve canlı performanslarla sürdürmektedir. İstanbul ve Diyarbakır'ın yanı sıra Avrupa'nın farklı kentlerinde de sahne alan sanatçı, çeşitli televizyon projelerinde rol almış ve program sunuculuğu yapmıştır.
Kamuya açık bilgilere göre Ceylan Kaya 43 yaşındadır. Ancak sanatçının kesin doğum tarihi hakkında doğrulanmış bir bilgi bulunmamaktadır.
Ceylan Kaya'nın aslen Tuncelili olduğu belirtilmektedir. Sanatçının doğduğu ilçe veya doğum yerine ilişkin net bilgi ise kamuya açık kaynaklarda yer almamaktadır.
Ceylan Kaya, müzik kariyerinin yanı sıra sunuculuk ve oyunculuk alanlarında da faaliyet göstermektedir. İstanbul, Diyarbakır, Frankfurt ve Lyon gibi şehirlerde sahne performansları sergileyen sanatçı, televizyon projelerinde de yer almıştır.
Kaya, Ceylan Kaya Show ve Akşam Sefası programlarında sunuculuk yapmıştır. Oyunculuk alanında ise çeşitli televizyon dizilerinde rol üstlenmiştir.
Müzik çalışmalarını sürdüren Ceylan Kaya'nın öne çıkan şarkıları arasında "Elimden Tut", "Şansı Yok", "Dönemem", "Nokta", "Bilakis Aşk" ve "Kan Çiçekleri" yer almaktadır. Sanatçının ayrıca 4 Te 4 adlı EP çalışması ve Turnam isimli albüm çalışması bulunmaktadır.
Ceylan Kaya'nın evli olup olmadığı, eşinin kim olduğu ve çocuk sahibi olup olmadığına ilişkin kamuya açık kaynaklarda doğrulanmış ayrıntılı bilgi bulunmamaktadır. Bu nedenle sanatçının medeni durumu ve aile yaşamı hakkında kesin bir bilgi vermek mümkün değildir.
Ceylan Kaya, Instagram'da @ceylankayaofficial kullanıcı adıyla yer almaktadır. Sanatçı, hesabı üzerinden sahne performanslarına ve güncel çalışmalarına ilişkin paylaşımlar yapmaktadır.

There Are Three things you don’t skimp on if you want a happy life: a good mattress , a good pair of shoes , and the best office chair you can find. Each is key to a world free of unnecessary pain. Finding the right ergonomic chair can be the difference between a satisfying and focused home office life and a squirmy day filled with cricks and small dissatisfactions.
The best desk chair is almost always an adjustable chair—one that can be tailored to your body’s unique shape and that offers enough lumbar support to avoid back problems even after long hours at the grind. Many chairs also utilize materials that can dissipate body heat, so you’re not stuck in Zoom meetings with a sweaty back. But the chair options out there can be bewildering. Luckily, the WIRED Reviews team has spent more than seven years sorting them out. WIRED Gear editor Julian Chokkattu has tested more than 60 chairs at his last tally. Reviewer Mathew Korfhage and other staffers have tried more than a dozen more, and most of our top picks have been tested by multiple people with different heights and body types.
WIRED’s favorite office chair for most people is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro ($499) because of its balance between value, features, comfort, and adjustability. That chair, and its lower-budget Ergonomic Chair ($369) cousin, have been tested and attested to by multiple WIRED reviewers. But we also offer chairs for every budget, from the preternaturally comfortable Steelcase Gesture ($1,510) to a $150 chair from Staples that leaves cheap Amazon brands in the dust.
We all have differing body types and needs, which is why we’ve put together a broad collection of recommendations—and why we enlist people of all sizes to keep testing our top picks for comfort and durability. Hopefully, we have a home office chair for you here.
For more home office buying guides, check out our Best Standing Desks , Best Laptop Stands , Best Home Office Gear , Best Mechanical Keyboards , and Best Webcams guides.
Updated October 2026: We tested the newly released Humanscale Freedom Ocean Headrest and added it as WIRED’s favorite reclining chair. We also added the Sihoo Doro C300 and Amseatac Crisscross Chair, streamlined our top picks, updated links and pricing throughout, and removed discontinued items.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
The price of a good office chair often inspires actual gasps, easily cresting $1,000. This is typically justified. Most cheaper chairs reveal their shortcomings quickly and uncomfortably. Branch’s Ergonomic Chair Pro is WIRED’s top pick for most people in part because it’s available at an attainable price while still offering comfort, ergonomics, and build quality. At $499, it’s not egregiously expensive and it has a decent warranty period.
One of the main markers of a good office chair is how well it can be adjusted to fit your particular shape and size. This is where Branch’s Ergonomic Chair Pro excels. The armrests can move up and down, forward and back, and angle inward or outward. But unlike most comparable chairs, the arms of the armrests can also move in and out to accommodate wider or narrower bodies, and lock into place.
The seat depth can also be pushed out if you’re tall, or pulled in if you’re short. The Pro can lock into the upright position, or at a few different reclining angles. This seat tilt allows for a more active seating position when you’re grinding away—a vanishingly rare feature. The high-density foam cushion is decently soft, noted tester Julian Chokkattu, who appreciated how the mesh backrest was able to follow the curve of his back. The lumbar support can also be adjusted deeper or shallower. (Chokkattu and I both tend to like more aggressive lumbar support, but it can take getting used to for a lot of people.)
The stock Branch seat might be a bit short for those above 6 feet tall, but this is fixable with a $29 add-on Tall Cylinder . You can also add a headrest, though Chokkattu did not find it was needed. Other options include personalized picks on fabric, vegan leather, or leather-leather.
It’s sturdy and well-built, with a powder-coated aluminum base and casters that roll easily on hardwood. Drawbacks are few, though Chokkattu found that the recline tension knob didn’t do much in particular. —Matthew Korfhage
Steelcase’s Gesture is comfortable, no matter how you’re sitting. It’s an attractive chair, too, with several colorful upholstery options. The seat is cushy, and while some might find it thin, it feels plush compared to the even pricier Herman Miller Embody (see below). I like how you can extend the seat depth forward with a twist of a knob—super elegant, which is a good descriptor for the Gesture on the whole. The recline knob smartly offers a series of clicks to indicate the angles you can lock, and even adjusting the armrests—whether you want to move them up and down, left and right, or forward and back—is fluid without any jerky movements.
The backrest aligns nicely with my back, and you can grab the tabs to adjust the lumbar support to hit the curve of your spine. All this makes for a comfortable sitting experience, even more so with the headrest upgrade. I typically don’t care for a headrest, but I used it here more than any other chair. It sticks forward quite a bit, so I don’t need to lean my head back as far to let it rest. Assembly was easy, too; it’s simply placing the seat pan on the legs because the backrest and seat were already preassembled. The only thing to note is that since this is an all-foam chair, you may run warm, especially in the summer, unless you can crank the AC to keep your home office cool.
Another downside is that the Gesture’s upholstery may not hold up well over time, at least not as long as a seat like the Herman Miller Embody. I haven’t seen this on my test model, but our original reviewer noted it, and a friend who has owned a Gesture for several years also complained about it. — Julian Chokkattu
The Branch Ergonomic Chair was WIRED’s previous top pick for most people, before getting displaced by the much-improved adjustability and lumbar support of the Pro. But the Ergonomic Chair is still a great place to start if you’re on a tight budget. The chair assembles in minutes, with the help of the—surprisingly rare—actually intuitive instructions.
While the original Ergonomic does not offer the 14-point adjustability of the armrests on the Pro, you can still push the armrests forward and back, up and down; extend or push the seat in; or lock the recline. Adjustable lumbar support is also on offer, and the chair looks sleek—with a number of colors to choose from and an optional headrest. At its price, this is an impressive offering.
Note that the Pro’s forward tilt option is absent here, and so active sitters might find that the chair doesn’t keep your back as upright as you’d like. The OG chair also doesn’t offer a longer cylinder for taller people. But after years of testing, 6’ 4” tester Chokkattu still found the chair comfortable —as did his 5’ 1” partner. The double-woven nylon mesh backrest feels nice to lean against. The seat is made of firm, comfortable high-density foam, and doesn’t trap heat as much as many other foam seats we’ve tested.
Fair warning, though: In Chokkattu’s experience, the chair’s material can be a magnet for pet hair. If you have a cat or a dog who loves you too much, you may want to invest in a nice pet vacuum . The fabric on the front end of the seat can also pill a bit. — Matthew Korfhage
It might take you a week or two (or even a month) to get used to the Herman Miller Embody, but it’s well worth your patience. I always return to the Embody after testing other chairs, and it feels like a breath of fresh air every time. Its upright positioning supports my back well and eases lingering back pain from years of sitting in a cheap gaming chair. The seat feels rigid at first, but eventually becomes surprisingly pillowy, and the armrests…

Exclusive: Investigation finds at least 25 cases affected by AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes
Undisclosed AI use has affected more than two dozen court cases this year, prompting judges to complain about AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, an investigation has revealed.
Proceedings where judges have been forced to deal with lawyers, police officers and claimants misusing the technology in 2026 include a high court dispute between tax lawyers marred by what the judge called “unacceptable” use of “generative AI hallucinations” and references to nonexistent cases.
Another involved a police officer in a grievous bodily harm case who used AI to write a witness statement so it would maximise the attacker’s sentence and “make a judge … weep”. A barrister in a $21m (£16m) high court dispute between two Nigerian oil companies made an argument based on a ruling – supposedly by a senior judge – that had been entirely invented by a hallucinating AI, leading the judge to warn of “the dangers of relying on the product of AI without verification”.
The spate of cases in which problems with AI tools have occurred in 2026 – at least 25, according to a trawl of published judgments by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism shared with the Guardian – comes despite a series of warnings from senior legal figures about the danger of the technology when used to cut corners and build cases. Brett Dixon, the president of the Law Society, told the Guardian AIs producing verbose case documents, particularly when non-lawyers represent themselves, is also taking up more of judges’ time, undermining efforts to clear court backlogs.
“You go from three pages from a lawyer … using human judgment to a rambling 60 pages from a commercial AI,” he said.
Last week, the supreme court judge Lord Sales also said the supreme court was growing “increasingly concerned” about AI and highlighted fears the technology could leave the legal profession deskilled.
“The danger is not simply that the machine gets the answer wrong,” he said. “The greater long-term danger is that human beings gradually lose the ability to know whether it has got the answer wrong.”
Cases affected by AI this year often involved people representing themselves, but also legal professionals increasingly using the technology to accelerate research, save time and increase earnings. Earlier this month the problem hit the Crown Prosecution Service when one of its lawyers cited an imaginary legal precedent .
Among the cases so far in 2026 a senior insolvency judge, Mark Mullen, discovered a junior solicitor had relied on an AI chatbot to research a point of law and took its invented quote from a fictitious statute. The judge examined the AI chat logs and discovered it had produced “nonsense” and warned in his judgment “AI has the potential to be wholly unreliable”.
In another case, the court of appeal dismissed an application for a convicted criminal from Derbyshire to challenge a four-year prison sentence for crimes including grievous bodily harm. The man had pleaded guilty after smashing his way through a glass patio door with a shovel to get into a house where the mother of his children had barricaded herself with a friend and her child. He threatened them with a large kitchen knife, fled and in the process broke a police officer’s shoulder.
The investigating police officer created a victim personal statement (VPS) by uploading a transcript of the mother’s interviews to Microsoft’s Copilot AI and prompting it “to achieve the highest sentence and the most tear-jerking VPS to make a judge or reader weep when reading”.
After the officer was removed from frontline duty the appeal court judges warned that “that no police officer should ever prepare a witness statement of any kind in this way”.
“We have seen how vulnerable the court system is to the introduction of AI,” said Brian Flanagan, associate professor at the school of law and criminology at Maynooth University. “It is always going to be very tempting and people will continue to produce fabricated authorities and that’s pretty serious.”
Last month, the Civil Justice Council recommended that witnesses of fact in civil cases must sign a declaration that their statements had not been prepared through the use of an AI tool that had generated or influenced its substantive content – including facts, reasoning, arguments and opinions. The CJC’s working group, led by Sir Colin Birss, the second most senior judge in England and Wales, also highlighted the urgent need for guidance on the use of AI by non-lawyers who are representing themselves in the courts – known as litigants in person.
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the growing use of AI in our courts and we’re taking steps to ensure any use of the technology is safe, appropriate, and properly controlled. That includes boosting the support given to courts through additional judges, legal officers, modern case management systems, and remote hearing technology.”

Repeated construction-zone violations and a California DMV ban have forced the autonomous vehicle giant off the freeway for the second time this year.
Most people know not to try to pass highway patrol cars while performing a traffic break on a freeway. But on November 6th, a driverless Waymo on Interstate 280 failed that test.
Video shows the robotaxi attempting to overtake two California Highway Patrol cruisers during a traffic break, a moving violation that could get a human driver’s license suspended. For Waymo, it was the latest in a series of freeway blunders that eventually led to the California DMV last week banning its vehicles from all state interstates .
Construction zones have also posed a challenge. Between October and November 2026, the company reported a total of 11 instances in which its vehicles failed to recognize that a freeway lane was closed because of construction and drove into the restricted area anyway, according to a recently filed recall .
With all these violations piling up, Waymo decided last week to pause commercial freeway rides across all of its US markets. It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules.
For years, the autonomous vehicle industry assumed freeways would be the easy part — no jaywalkers, no unprotected left turns — while dense cities were seen as the ultimate battle. Yet Waymo has flipped that script, racking up millions of urban miles while repeatedly stumbling on the interstate.
It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules
This was neither the first time Waymo was forced to pause freeway operations nor the first time it had been caught blundering into construction sites. Earlier this year, the company temporarily halted freeway rides after its robotaxis entered active construction zones in Arizona and California. It issued a recall in June and gradually resumed freeway operations starting in late July after updating its software.
But experts note that the recall didn’t work, as evidenced by the subsequent violations.
”The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway,” says Phil Koopman, emeritus professor in electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and a researcher specializing in autonomous vehicle safety.
In an interview, Koopman says Waymo is using recalls as “Band-Aids,” which he argues doesn’t really address the root of the problem. In addition to the freeway snafus, Waymo also filed a recall related to the intersection crash where its vehicle failed to detect a police officer directing traffic. In short, the car followed the officer’s orders until passing traffic blocked its view, at which point its software lost track of the “stop” command and drove into the intersection on its own, the company said in the recall report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Waymo later updated its software across its entire fleet so the vehicles remember manual traffic signals even when an officer is temporarily blocked from view.
There have been other recalls related to Waymo passing stopped school buses and driving through flooded roadways . This has led Koopman to theorize that rather than solving the underlying perception and reasoning flaws, Waymo is using “dynamic geofencing” to route around known flood zones or using real-time GPS feeds of school buses until a car encounters an unmapped situation.
“The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway.”
“It felt to me like they were really not being able to fix these problems,” he says. “They’re putting Band-Aids on and getting on with scaling.”
In response to the California DMV order, Waymo said it’s working closely with regulators on a solution, noting that its vehicles haven’t crashed or injured anyone while driving through restricted areas on the freeway.
“Our ridehailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week,” Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas said last week. “We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”
Since its inception, Waymo has typically avoided highways, opting instead for longer routes that stick to local roads when ferrying passengers. This has not gone unnoticed by the company’s customers , who often complain their trips can take longer because the vehicles are prohibited from using routes that travel on highways. But in late 2025, Waymo said it was ready to hit the highway.
“Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master when we’re talking about full autonomy without a human driver as a backup,” Dmitri Dolgov, co-CEO of Waymo, said in a November 2025 briefing with reporters . “And at scale. So it took time to do it properly with a strong focus on system safety and reliability.”
“Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master.”
Now it seems as if Waymo may have jumped the gun. The company’s decision to pull back from the freeway, twice in one year, reflects the enormous stakes of operating driverless vehicles at high speeds. At 10 to 25 mph on a city street, applying the brakes solves almost any confusion, and crash lethality is drastically lower. At 60 or 70 mph, stopping distances stretch out, and any mistake involving a roadside worker or stranded motorist is nearly 100 percent fatal. And if the vehicle gets confused and needs to ping a remote operator for assistance, the latency of that connection and the time it takes to receive a reply becomes a major liability.
Koopman thinks that subtle edge cases — like a gap in construction cones or a cop’s hand gesture — are tripping Waymo up right after its transition to end-to-end machine learning . Unlike older modular systems where engineers could write explicit rules, statistical models struggle when familiar objects appear in unfamiliar contexts.
“If you’ve trained on the individual elements, their combination presents a special meaning that is different than usual,” he says. “A stop sign folded out on a school bus is completely different from a stop sign on a post... Everything I’ve seen is consistent with the hypothesis that it’s having trouble with subtle contextual clues.”
For Waymo, solving for the freeway is essential if the company wants to continue expanding its service area to include popular ridehailing destinations, like airports. Waymo’s future reliability will depend on it. While safety engineers want to do the right thing, executives face massive market pressure to ship “good enough” fixes and apologize later, Koopman argues. And because traffic tickets and standard fines don’t deter well-capitalized tech giants like Alphabet, regulators need mandatory public transparency — not quiet software patches via recalls.
“If DMV gets a neutral look without political pressure, they’re going to say, ‘Fool me once, shame on you,’” Koopman says. “They can’t just accept Waymo saying, ‘Trust us, bro, we fixed it this time for sure.’”

The best MagSafe wallets are compact, slim and svelte, and attach securely to your iPhone (or MagSafe-compatible case). These can be handy if you just want to carry a few cards, like your work badge or your train fare, or if you want to forgo carrying a traditional wallet entirely. MagSafe wallets are great for anyone who wants to travel light and needs only a couple of cards at a time. We’ve tested dozens, and our favorites are below.
Read our MagSafe guides for more useful accessory recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Accessories , Best MagSafe Power Banks , Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers , and Best MagSafe Grips .
Updated July 2026: I’ve added new wallets from Moft, ESR, and Journey. I’ve also checked for accuracy throughout.
MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12 , iPhone 13 , iPhone 14 , iPhone 15 , iPhone 16 , and iPhone 17 ranges (excluding the iPhone 16e ). It comprises of a ring of magnets on the back of the phone, and it was developed to create a faster, more precise wireless charging system. Those magnets on the back also connect to different accessories, such as external batteries, car mounts, and wallets.
If you use a case on your iPhone, you will need to make sure it’s also MagSafe (the case itself will have a ring of magnets inside it). This will ensure a proper connection with MagSafe accessories. If you use a non-MagSafe case, the connection will be very weak, and MagSafe products may just slide off your iPhone. We have lots of case recommendations in our guides:
When buying a wallet, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2 connections. It should indicate this prominently in the product description. Qi2 is the wireless charging standard, and all MagSafe iPhones support Qi2. Android phones now also support Qi2 and some have magnets inside, like the Google Pixel 10 series .
MagSafe wallets come with the same ring of magnets that allow them to snap onto the back of the iPhone directly or onto a MagSafe or Qi2 case. This gives the wallet a strong and secure hold on your device. The wallets we’ve included in this guide all have the MagSafe seal of approval.
Apple first introduced MagSafe for its iPhones in 2020. The following models support the technology:
To use a MagSafe wallet with an Android phone (or the iPhone 16e ), you’ll need to use a MagSafe case . Several case manufacturers have started adding a ring of magnets to Android phone cases in order to port over the same magnetic experience native to iPhones. We have guides to cases designed for top Android phone models featuring magnetic options that should play nicely with third-party MagSafe wallets.
No, MagSafe will not demagnetize your credit cards. Credit cards have magnetic stripe encoding that’s strong enough to keep them from being demagnetized, and MagSafe wallets in this guide come with a built-in shield designed to keep your cards safe. However, you may run into issues with hotel key cards and some gift cards. Keep those away as a precaution.
I use a MagSafe wallet every day as my primary wallet. I check that it snaps onto the iPhone or MagSafe case firmly—and that it doesn’t slide off when taking my phone out of my pocket, bag, or jacket. I also make sure cards fit well into the sleeve and that they don’t fall out. I only recommend wallets that feel durable, are easy to use, and can hold the standard amount of cards (at least two to three).
UAG’s Metropolis MagSafe wallet is on the spendier side, but you won’t be replacing it in a year or two. It is lightweight yet robust with Kevlar construction. There’s a large slot on the back that can hold up to three cards, and you can unfold the wallet and store an additional three (or cash) inside. It also pulls double duty as a stand if you need to prop up your phone, and you can orient your phone in landscape or portrait mode. — Molly Higgins
Smartish’s MagSafe wallet makes me wish all wallets had a slot on the side to push out the cards. I never had to take it off my phone to access cards. Just give the spacious side opening a little push with your thumb, and the cards slide out. My cards remained secure, and I never had an issue with them falling out. It’s made of vegan leather, and Smartish offers a few fun designs. — Brenda Stolyar
This luxe, super-thin leather MagSafe wallet from Nomad has Apple’s Find My feature built in, so you can easily locate it in the Find My app if it’s misplaced. That does mean you need to charge the wallet, but don’t worry, there's no proprietary cable here. Instead, the wallet can be wirelessly charged on any MagSafe or Qi2 charger; once it’s fully charged, the battery lasts for five months. Easy peasy.
It’s made from vegetable-tanned Horween leather with a polycarbonate frame, and it can hold up to four cards. It looks classy, and it’s great for anyone with a tendency to lose things. —Molly Higgins
Note that Nomad also sells a dedicated tracker card , which can add Find My to any wallet but will take up valuable space in a MagSafe version.
I love this wallet from Moft, which is compatible with Apple Find My so you always know where it is. It’s relatively standard-looking, but it has a built-in tripod, which came in handy numerous times when I wanted to film a quick outfit check or take a group photo. It raises your phone camera to 8 inches high, and the wallet is very sturdy, so you can dial in the right angle. It works in landscape or portrait orientation. With space for two cards, it isn’t the roomiest but is rich in features.
You can always rely on Casetify for unique designs. Its Snappy MagSafe wallet is available in various styles and colors. It’s slim, durable, and sleek—the illustrations haven’t faded after months of use. It’s made from vegan leather (aka plastic), but Casetify uses BioVeg , derived from recycled polyester and vegetable oil from non-food and GMO-free corn crops .
It can hold up to three cards, and there’s a built-in shield that protects them from magnetic damage. My only gripe is that it can be a little difficult to pull the cards out when the wallet is attached to your phone or case. I typically have to detach it and use the opening from the back to slide out the cards. — Brenda Stolyar
Ridge’s metal MagSafe wallet feels solid and high-quality. A few of us tested it, and it reliably held our setups, including one tester’s daily carry of eight cards plus a thicker tracking card. The magnets could be stronger, but Ridge does sell a strengthening tray that might be useful if you’re concerned.
This wallet can be a little weird to use at first, but you build up muscle memory quickly. There’s a finger slot for pushing cards out, and you slide them back in on the opposite side. Ridge also includes a Torx screwdriver and extra screws, which are useful for switching out the plates, adding or subtracting room for cards, or adding on accessories like the brand’s wallet chain or cash strap . — Louryn Strampe
Most MagSafe wallets are designed to hold just a few cards, but I love the Moft Snap Field because it can hold so much more. You get plenty of storage space for cards—technically up to eight cards, though more reasonably seven—alongside a dedicated slot for an extra SIM card and a SIM card ejector.
That extra room already puts the Snap Field a step ahead of most other MagSafe wallets, but you can also store just about anything you want inside. It uses a folding design held together by magnets, so you can quickly throw in cash, coins, or paper cards. Regardless of what you store inside, you can easily get to your cards with a pull tab. And, if all of that wasn’t enough, the backing that attaches to your phone can pop out and function as a kickstand. — Jacob Roach

Picking a gaming mouse can be difficult. There are countless metrics to factor in and a nearly unlimited number of mice with unique approaches in defining what's best. Quite honestly, it’s a market rife with opportunities for analysis paralysis to take hold.
That’s why I take the time to test countless gaming mice—to tell you what works and what doesn’t. I can’t say precisely which mouse will work for you—that’s dependent not only on technical specs but on your preferences, needs, budget, and hand size—but hopefully I can provide some insights into the top options out there, what's the best for specific types of gamers, and why I’ve picked them.
Be sure to read our other peripheral buying guides for more, including the Best Ergonomic Mouse , Best Gaming Headsets , Best Mechanical Keyboards , and Best Hall Effect Keyboards .
Updated November 2026: I've added the Razer Basilisk V4 Pro and Wallhack M-001. I've also included the Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike in my honorable mentions, reorganized the list, and updated prices.
The Razer Cobra HyperSpeed (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is far more reasonable and practical than most of the ultra-light options today. Instead of shaving down features and mass to make the simplest mouse possible, the Cobra Hyperspeed finds an ideal middle ground, maintaining features like RGB lighting, Bluetooth connectivity, and options for wireless charging. Despite that, it still weighs below 70 grams, a number that was unbelievable for even the most premium wireless mice a decade ago. Inside, it’s packing an optical sensor, optical switches, and an optical scroll wheel—all top-of-the-line parts that are some of the fastest and most reliable on the market. While the mouse is limited to 1,000-Hz polling with the included low-profile USB-A dongle (which I prefer for convenience), it can be upgraded to 8,000 Hz with the bulkier and less-convenient HyperPolling dongle , cutting out its only serious limitation.
Beyond that, this mouse can do practically everything. It works as a travel mouse, a permanent desktop solution, and is even compatible with Razer’s wireless charging pucks , which lets you charge the mouse using either the Mouse Dock Pro , which ups your polling rate to 8,000 Hz, or the HyperFlux V2 wireless charging mousepad. The simple, symmetrical shape is comfortable and easy to hold, with the curved buttons on top creating spots to rest your fingers, while the low, gradual curve feels natural for resting your palm. Plus, its near-symmetry means it can be used as an ambidextrous mouse in a pinch (although lefties will miss out on the side buttons).
While the price may be steep, Wallhack’s M-001 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best I’ve tested in a long time. Although the specs aren’t quite cutting-edge (the sensor is a bit outdated, and some of the internals are still mechanical instead of optical), every aspect of this mouse’s user experience has been fine-tuned to perfection. That's what sets it apart for me.
The mouse itself is made entirely from magnesium, and the outer shell doesn’t feature any of the large weight-saving cutouts used by similar mice from Corsair, AngryMiao, and even Razer. Instead, the upper is entirely solid, and all of the cutouts are on the underside of the mouse. Because of this, the battery can be swapped out within seconds.
Alongside the mouse itself, the M-001’s dongle is one of the best on the market. Instead of simply sitting on a desk, this dongle incorporates physical dials to adjust the mouse’s sensitivity and polling rate, and recharges the spare battery when not in use.
While it may be silly, my favorite feature of this mouse is the swappable batteries themselves. Similar to a Nintendo Switch cartridge or an SD card, the batteries feature a push-lock mechanism that’s robust, satisfying, and intuitive, improving significantly on the magnet or rotation-lock systems that other swappable mouse batteries use.
The Rival 3 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is a simple, no-frills gaming mouse. It’s lightweight, robust, and pretty much hits all the marks for gaming: Easy-access side buttons, clicky main buttons, underside RGB lighting, and a grippy rubberized scroll wheel. This SteelSeries mouse doesn’t innovate much, but like a Toyota Camry, it’s simple and reliable enough to get nearly anything done. At a price below $50, you’re getting all the performance you can realistically use for non-professional gaming. There aren’t any unnecessary features that add complication, and the mouse can be fully disassembled in under five minutes with a set of Phillips and Torx screwdrivers.
The Razer Viper V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the latest installment in a long line of fantastic competitive mice, offering performance improvements across every metric. Along with top-of-the-line specs, optical sensors across the board, and a great symmetrical shape, the V4 also incorporates the same spherical dongle included with the Deathadder V4 Pro, which maintains its 8,000-Hz polling while adding LED indicators for information like connection quality, battery life, and DPI stage.
Using the exact same shape as the V3, this mouse is comfortable and intuitive to use. The shape is easy to move around, with small curves on the mouse buttons for your fingertips to rest, and the curvature of the sides creates natural spots for your thumb and pinky. The Razer Synapse software is one of the most powerful and intuitive on the market. There are customization options for mouse dpi, tracking distance, dynamic sensitivity, and even adjusting the mouse sensor to accommodate a rotated grip.
The only downside of the Viper V4 Pro is how uncompromising it is— there's no Bluetooth, and the included 2.4-GHz dongle requires a USB-A to USB-C cable (included) that runs to your computer, with no option for a smaller USB-A dongle (last seen on the V2). These decisions were made to lighten the mouse and improve connection quality, but they can be inconvenient if you need a wireless gaming mouse to pair with a laptop.
The Infinity .97 is one of the lightest mice I’ve tested at only 48.3 grams (without the removable rear panel, which adds 3.8 grams), and one of the sturdiest thanks to its magnesium upper shell. While the skeletal shape may look off-putting at first, it was far more comfortable and usable than I would have expected, especially when used with a fingertip grip. However, anyone dedicated to a palm or claw grip will likely be better served by a larger mouse with a sturdier back end.
Beyond weight, this mouse has fantastic specs: 8,000-Hz polling, optical switches, and a rating of 0.2 ms of latency all put it on par with Razer and Logitech’s best offerings. The most impressive feature by far is the removable and magnetically hot-swappable batteries that recharge using the mouse’s 2.4G dongle. This eliminates downtime from a dead battery and reduces the risks of long-term battery degradation and failure (assuming AngryMiao continues to sell spares ).
While the styling is certainly more of an acquired taste, the large gaps result in a shape that’s rigid and better-looking than the usual uniform, hexagon-shaped holes. The shape is shockingly comfortable despite the gaps (which are placed to preserve typical touch points), and the removable rear “hatchback” panel finds a reasonable balance between a standard shape and the ultra-lightweight “fingertip mice” that have become more popular in recent years.
The software is also shockingly robust, with expected adjustments for DPI, polling, macros, and so on, alongside more granular adjustments like debounce speed, motion sync, ripple correction, and a Blast Mode that sets the mouse’s internal sensor to its maximum speed of 20,000 Hz. (It’s worth noting that the mouse still communicates with your computer at 8,000 Hz—this simply provides more data from the sensor to the mouse). Also, unlike some similarly-priced offerings, this mouse has both 2.4G and Bluetooth connectivity.

Google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto. If the switch hasn’t happened yet on your own vehicle’s dashboard, then it should happen soon.
You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the new “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.
If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else , then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant. It's a truly natural conversation partner that can dig deep into information available online, and respond to a much wider range of queries. Here's what the upgraded app can do specifically when you're traveling on the road.
All of the standard commands you might have already been using are still here, of course, like "navigate home" or “Where's the nearest Walmart?” With Gemini though, there's much more flexibility in what you can say without the AI getting confused or misunderstanding what you're asking about.
For example, your questions can be multilayered. Something like "find the nearest coffee shop that has a drive-thru and is open now" will look for those exact criteria. You're also able to ask context-sensitive follow-up questions, such as "What time will it shut?" or "How long will it take to get there?" if you need further details.
You can ask more general questions too, such as "tell me more about the place I'm heading to" or "Is there outdoor seating?” But bear in mind that Gemini will be limited to scouring the data on Google Maps for its information. (It's a disembodied AI that's never been anywhere.) If it doesn't know the answer to something, it should tell you that.
Overall, it's smarter in every aspect. I was recently navigating a difficult junction and couldn't work out whether the map was sending me left or right. I asked Gemini, "Will I be traveling east or west after the next turn?" and it figured out the answer. That helped me avoid veering off in the wrong direction.
One of the major benefits of having a voice-controlled AI in the car is having it handle messaging and audio tasks without you needing to take your eyes off the road or fish around for a button. If you tell Gemini to “read my last message,” it'll speak it out for you and give you the opportunity to reply. You can also specify the app, otherwise Google Messages will be used by default—Google Chat and WhatsApp are among the others that are supported.
Gemini is able to give you summaries of group chats, which is really handy when you're on a drive and the conversations you're involved in are building up message after message that you can't check. Name a group chat in a supported app and ask for a summary, or just request summaries of unread messages. You'll be able to get the gist without checking each individual message.
The usual array of audio commands are here, carried over from Google Assistant, so you can quickly start or stop audio in your music, podcast, radio, and audiobook apps. As well as continuing from where you left off, you can also name artists, albums, and playlists that you want to queue up. YouTube Music and Spotify are among the apps supported, if you need to specify one.
Another extra from Gemini is being able to ask about the artist or song that's currently playing, and get more information on it. You might want to learn the history of a particular band, find out how long a certain song was at number one, or even get recommendations based on what's currently playing—just ask Gemini.
Much more than Google Assistant, Gemini can help you learn something or develop some ideas while you're behind the wheel. If you're on the way to a movie premiere, you can ask Gemini about the history of the film, the director, and the actors, and it'll remember the context of your conversation. (It'll all get synced back to the Gemini app on your other devices.)
Voice commands such as “help me prepare for my interview” or “come up with ideas for a quick and easy meal to make for dinner" will initiate a chat with Gemini that you can continue throughout your journey—and hopefully arrive well-prepared or with dinner sorted (or whatever it is). Maybe don’t ask about anything too mind-bending, as you’ll still need to concentrate on driving.
Gemini will ask along the way for any information it needs about what you’re interviewing for or the ingredients you’ve got at home. You can also ask Gemini to quiz you on a certain topic or run a query on something you see on the journey—like a landmark or a restaurant you go past.
Finally, there’s always the weather: Gemini will give you forecasts for the areas and specific locations you give it, on whatever day you want within the next week or so. Perhaps more useful for journeys are questions like “When is the rain going to stop?” or “What are the weather conditions like at my destination?” which will help you plan your trip.

The Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City. Fiat has been selling this tiny electric vehicle in Europe for three years, but it's now arriving in the US for $14,985 as a street-legal micromobility vehicle . Except it's more like a golf cart than a small EV.
It has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags. Classified as a “Low Speed Vehicle (LSV),” it can only operate on roads with a posted speed limit of 35 mph or less. (You still need a driver's license, and the Topolino must be registered and have auto insurance.) It also doesn't have a traditional EV charging plug ; instead, it uses a 10-foot AC plug that works in any wall outlet—which can be tough if you're in a Brooklyn apartment.
“It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA. “This segment of micromobility—and that's really golf carts—based on the data we have, it's going to grow 28 percent in the next 5 years. People are driving golf carts not to play golf—they're driving them to go to the beach, to go to the clubhouse, to go get coffee, dinner, but they're all just generic. Topolino adds a little bit of that Italian flair and charm, and it's just so unique.”
That’s hard to refute. There's nothing like the Topolino on the market, EV or otherwise. Its adorable looks have drawn the attention of passersby, who've flicked me a thumbs up as I drove past, or pulled out their phones to sneak a quick pic. The Topolino (which is Italian for “little mouse,” and also what Italians call Mickey Mouse ) comes with a lot of compromises, but I've had a blast piloting this thing around the city.
From my conversation with Waterhouse, it was clear that Fiat expects to sell more of these Topolino cars in places like suburban Florida. Gated communities, large residences with private land, homes by the beach— you get the idea . There are also hopes to turn the Topolino into a fleet vehicle for campuses and the like. But I wanted to see what it would be like in the bustling streets of New York City. After all, I already drive the Fiat 500 as my personal vehicle.
The Fiat Topolino, left, next to the already small Fiat 500, right.
The first thing that surprised me—other than the minuscule size, which you won't stop thinking about—is how plasticky the thing is. I leaned on it for a second and felt the plastic exterior sink in a little, which immediately made me realize the Topolino won't handle a crash very well; no crumple zones, no airbags—just seatbelts. So yes, don't take this thing on the highway.
It's built for two people and not much else. The passenger can stow a suitcase in front of them, and there's a rack on the back of the car to store another. But besides mesh pouches in the door frames and an elongated glove compartment on top of the dashboard that runs the width of the car, that's about it for storage.
I should also mention the Topolino comes in a few variants: The standard model I tried has full doors and a fixed glass roof, but there's an Open Air model with a roll-back soft-top roof, and the Dolce Vita model has rope doors (aka no doors) and the soft-top roof. You can buy the car in mint, orange, or brownish-gray.
Thankfully, despite my 6'4" frame, I fit quite comfortably in the Topolino. I do have to swing my leg under the steering wheel as I get in, and the seats are a little firm, but the inside feels quite roomy. Only the driver's seat can move forward or back—the passenger seat stays put, and you cannot adjust the steering wheel height.
The asymmetrical, reverse-hinged doors are very unique. The driver's side opens outward from the front, and the passenger door opens the opposite way. There's also a button on each side to open the door, and weirdly, to get out, you pull a fabric strap. Now, the driver-side strap is to the left of the steering wheel, which makes sense, but the passenger-side strap is in an awkward spot behind the seat, near the seatbelt strap. A few of my passengers found that annoying. Also annoying is that you need to use the key to unlock both doors individually—no auto-unlock button plus no key fob. (The car starts with a second key.)
The horizontally split, manually hinged windows flip up, but on rougher roads, they tend to flip back down. You can adjust the small, circular side mirrors and the rear-view mirror, which also doubles as a backup camera display. I have found the backup camera mostly useless, especially at night, when it's just really hard to see what’s going on.
Good thing visibility in the Topolino is excellent, so it's really easy to swing your head around. Unsurprisingly, you can park this thing anywhere. I've parallel parked the Topolino in several tight spots that no other car can fit in, and the lack of parking sensors or the lackluster backup camera didn't bother me. In a city as crowded as New York, that's incredibly valuable.
You should know there's no air-conditioning or heating. There's a windshield fan to defog the windows, which, along with the single wiper and wiper fluid, was useful on cold, rainy days. But in the winter months, you'll have to bundle up, or in the summer, affix a battery-powered (or USB-C) fan to the dashboard. On the dash, you have a simple instrument cluster that shows speed and remaining range, and a built-in phone mount to the right.
Turn the key to start the car, disengage the parking brake, and tap D or R to start driving. There's no power steering, so turning the wheel requires a little more force than you're used to, and the turn signals don't automatically disengage after you turn. Still, the car feels very responsive. The 8-horsepower electric motor feels fairly quick when you put the pedal to the metal, though you quickly hit the Topolino’s top speed. Good thing the default speed limit in New York City is 25 mph.
But as you start driving, you'll experience arguably the worst thing about the Fiat Topolino: the sound. Because of federal regulations around electric LSVs, the Topolino has a pedestrian alert sound—the kind of angelic hum you might have heard when an electric car is reversing or rolling up to a stop sign. Except the sound is constant, and it gets louder the faster you go. I'm not sure why it's so loud in the car. It feels like it's alerting me more than pedestrians around me.
The sound only disappears if you go past 22 mph, which isn't often, since streets in most cities have a stop sign or traffic light after every block. The first time my wife and I rode in the car, we could barely hear each other talk over the hum. You get used to it over time, but it's very annoying. You can try playing music over it, but the car has no speaker system. Instead, Fiat sells a pair of Monster Bluetooth speakers that you can magnetically stick to the top frame of the car. That works OK, but I didn't like having to keep them charged, so when they died, I played music from my phone. It was sad.
The ride is a little stiff. I drove over one of the worst roads in Brooklyn (Broadway), and you could feel every single bump. When I drove with my brother, they often just exclaimed “Jesus!” every few minutes. Cobblestone was equally pretty bad. But it's doable, and on well-maintained roads, the Topolino was a smooth ride.
New Yorkers rejoice! You legally cannot drive this car into New Jersey. (As if you needed a reason.) All of the bridges and tunnels to the Garden State have speed limits higher than 35 mph. However, I could take the East River bridges to go from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and I did exactly that. Driving over the Manhattan Bridge was a little terrifying when I was holding up a few cars in my lane and everyone decided to race around me. But I got a few thumbs-ups along the way, which helped. Everyone finds this car cute, which goes a long way toward how people treat you on the road.
As for range, it's not great. I wish it were closer to 80 miles instead of 46 miles, especially at this price. It's perfect for quick hour-long round trips around the…

Detailed estimate going back to 1800 shows how much carbon is being liberated.
Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.
A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.
Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.
Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO 2 emissions get turned way up.
The researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO 2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO 2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.
The simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO 2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO 2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.)
Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.
Regionally, over half of the total CO 2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.
Draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.
If peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.
But since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.
Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 ( About DOIs ).

Keyboards are important. Regardless of how little you might think about yours, you probably use it every day. A keyboard that’s comfortable and easy to use is indispensable and helps you not only do good work—but enjoy doing it as well.
Because we already have a separate guide focused on mechanical keyboards, this list instead places more focus on lower-profile keyboards and other non-mechanical options aimed at a more casual typist. There’s a greater focus on typing comfort and efficiency, instead of typing feel, and less emphasis on customization options like hot-swap sockets or keycap accessibility.
Be sure to check out our other peripheral guides for more, like the Best Mechanical Keyboards , Best Hall Effect Keyboards , Best Mouse , Best Ergonomic Mouse , and Best Computer Monitors .
Updated Noember 2026: I've added the Wallhack K-001 and Keychron K2 HE Concrete Edition to my top recommendations, as well as the Keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid to my honorable mentions. I've also included a couple of recent keyboards I've reviewed that I would suggest avoiding entirely.
One of the highlights of Keychron’s current lineup is its selection of mid-century-inspired keyboards with clean, simple designs and wood highlights. Instead of the standard gamer-y aesthetic, these keyboards offer a more refined style that looks at home on a professional’s desk. The K3 is the first low-profile keyboard in this series, offering a slimmer and more portable typing experience with the same fantastic design language. While this isn’t necessarily the best keyboard on this list by any one metric, I think it’s the most practical option for the largest number of users.
There are two versions of the K3: The typing-focused Ultra and the gaming-focused HE. The Ultra uses standard low-profile mechanical switches, with options for either linear Red switches, or tactile Brown or Banana switches. These switches can be swapped out without any soldering thanks to the hot-swap sockets on the PCB. The switches and stabilizers come lubed from the factory, resulting in typing that feels smooth and offers a consistent, rattle-free sound when typing.
The HE offers only linear Hall effect switches, but these allow for more advanced software customization, such as adjustable actuation distances (how far you press the switch before it registers an input) and Rapid Trigger (which allows for more rapid keypresses by detecting the direction of the switch’s movement). While the enhanced customization of a Hall effect switch is great for gaming, the adjustability won’t be worth the added cost and loss of switch customization for the average user.
The only trade-off with this keyboard is that, compared to a full-size mechanical keyboard, it does lose some travel distance; a low-profile switch is 3.1 mm total, compared with a standard switch’s 4.0 mm. This can be preferable for users who prefer a snappier typing experience or who prioritize a compact form factor.
Both models share the same compact form factor, stylish design, and open-source QMK software for customization, along with the ability to use Keychron’s web-based Launcher for adjusting key mapping and RGB lighting colors.
With Gateron-made KS-TR Hall effect switches and a design that looks straight out of a Dieter Rams–era Braun catalog, I absolutely love this keyboard. The typing experience is fantastic, and this keyboard has a presence on your desk that not many others can match. While the K-001 doesn’t feature a bouncy gasket-mount design, the “stack mount” system it uses (similar to the Wooting 60HE V2 listed below) creates a stiffer, consistent typing feel across the entire keyboard, which I prefer for regular typing.
Beyond that, the K-001 features specs that are competitive with quite a few high-end gaming offerings, with customizable settings for switch actuation distance, rapid trigger functionality, and extensive programmability. It even boasts an 8,000-Hz polling rate and 0.125-millisecond input latency, making it a fantastic choice for even the most competitive gaming. Really, the only thing missing is wireless connectivity, but that’s not a major issue for a gaming-focused keyboard with a hefty CNC aluminum shell.
Another small detail I love is the lighting on this keyboard. Each of the switches is designed to carefully guide the LED underneath to only shine behind the lettering, without any light bleeding between the keys. The LEDs themselves are a well-balanced, neutral white, as opposed to the multicolored RGB found in most keyboards (which often gain a very bluish tint when set to pure white). This all results in a much more minimal and tasteful LED setup compared to the ultra-bright, sometimes overwhelming offerings from other manufacturers.
While the price point is high, especially compared to offerings from more cost-conscious brands like Keychron, this keyboard really is a great object to hold and use, and one that has incredibly robust construction and great engineering underneath the hood.
Keychron’s B2 Pro is one of the best scissor-switch keyboards available, mainly because of the customization it allows. This keyboard uses Keychron’s Launcher, an in-browser software that provides extensive and intuitive customization options for its keyboards, with everything from remapping and macros to multiple function layers. For any type of productivity work, this level of customization can be a great way to optimize an already-good keyboard to one that's perfect for your regular tasks, whether that’s mapping multimedia controls to a function layer or having specific key combinations ready at a moment’s notice.
This keyboard offers a good typing experience for the price, using low-profile scissor switches with a short and snappy key press without being particularly loud or disruptive. The case is made entirely of plastic, and the keycaps are subtly sculpted with a dish (similar to Logitech’s MX Keys line), which makes finding the center of a keycap easier when touch-typing. Because of the low-profile scissor switches, the B2 Pro still feels like a laptop keyboard at the end of the day, which can seem lacking if you’re coming from something with a more robust design.
Slim, durable, and highly customizable, Razer’s Joro is pretty much the most compact gaming keyboard you can find today. It’s thinner than a laptop and just barely thicker than an iPhone, and has the same footprint as a standard 60 percent keyboard, meaning it can slip easily into a backpack, tote bag, or even a large purse. If you were really dedicated, I’m sure it could even fit in the pocket of some cargo pants. The Joro uses Razer’s Synapse software, an incredibly powerful and intuitive customization app that lets you control the keyboard’s RGB lighting, remap any of its keys, and program macros with ease.
The only significant downside of this keyboard is the lack of a 2.4-GHz dongle. This means the keyboard can connect only to devices via Bluetooth or a wired connection. While this isn’t a deal-breaker for me, since the device still has multi-device Bluetooth connectivity, it does slightly hinder the keyboard’s functionality.
In many ways, the Mchose GX87 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is a “mini” version of the WobKey Crush 80. It has the same layout with similar design choices, and it uses comparable switches and an identical gasket-mount system. However, the GX87 misses out on some of the fancier features of the Crush 80. The colors are e-coated instead of anodized on most models (which creates a less smooth texture), the case is lighter and simpler, and disassembly is generally more complicated.
However, this keyboard still feels great to type on, especially at its budget-minded starting price. If you’re less concerned about some of the style or convenience aspects of a keyboard but still want something that feels great while you're typing, the GX87 is one of the best options available from a per-dollar standpoint.
